title: How would you diagnose a React memory leak?
description: Learn systematic memory-leak diagnosis in React: heap snapshots, detached DOM nodes, uncleared subscriptions, and closure-based accumulation patterns.

data.text: A memory leak in a React app means something is holding a reference to a component, its closures, or a DOM node after the component unmounts. Over time, the heap grows, garbage collection runs more frequently, and eventually the tab crashes or the browser slows down. The fix is always the same: break the reference. The challenge is finding it.

data.title: What to look for
items: Event listeners added to `window` or `document` without cleanup in `useEffect`
WebSocket or EventSource connections left open
Subscriptions (RxJS, Firebase, Pusher) not unsubscribed in cleanup
Closures capturing large objects inside `setInterval` or `requestAnimationFrame`
Detached DOM nodes: React removes them, but a JS variable still references them

terms.definition: A DOM element no longer attached to the document but still referenced by JavaScript, preventing garbage collection.
Chrome DevTools captures all JS objects in memory. Comparing snapshots before and after an action shows what was retained unexpectedly.
A function that captures variables from its outer scope. If that function outlives the component, the captured variables stay in memory.
The total memory held by an object and everything it references. A small object can have a large retained size.

data.title: Using Chrome DevTools
items: Open Memory tab → Take a heap snapshot with the page in a clean state
Perform the action suspected to leak (navigate, open/close a modal, switch tabs)
Compare snapshots: look for 'Detached HTMLDivElement' or 'closure' entries that grew significantly
Double-click a suspect node to see its retainers—what is still pointing to it
Cross-reference with your code: find which effect or callback is keeping it alive

data.title: Leak: interval not cleared on unmount
data.content: The component sets an interval on mount but never clears it. After unmount, the interval callback still fires and holds a reference to the component's state.

data.title: Fix: always return a cleanup function
data.content: The `useEffect` cleanup runs before unmount and before the next effect run, breaking the reference.

data.text: React 18 Strict Mode double-invokes effects in development. If your cleanup is missing, you'll see duplicate intervals or subscriptions immediately. This is a feature, not a bug—it exposes leaks before production. Always test with Strict Mode enabled.

data.title: The fetch-in-interval trap
data.text: If `fetch` inside `setInterval` uses a stale closure, each callback captures the `setPrice` from the render when the interval was created. After unmount, the interval keeps firing and each call allocates a Promise. This pattern is especially dangerous in long-lived SPAs where mount/unmount happens repeatedly.

In Chrome DevTools Memory panel, select 'Detached DOM tree' in the Allocation instrumentation on timeline view. You'll see DOM nodes that were removed from the document but not garbage collected. The 'Retainers' panel shows the JavaScript path keeping them alive—often a global variable, a closure, or a third-party library's internal map.

items.text: Every `addEventListener` has a matching `removeEventListener` in the cleanup return
items.hint: Use the same handler reference—don't define the handler inline
Store the ID in a ref if the callback references changing state

items.text: WebSocket and EventSource are closed in cleanup
items.hint: Check for `.close()` calls in the return function
Use `takeUntil` with a `Subject` for RxJS; call `unsubscribe()` for Firebase

items.text: Large objects in closures are not captured unnecessarily
items.hint: If the interval only needs a small value, extract just that value into the closure

items.question: What's the difference between a memory leak and slow memory growth?
items.answer: A leak is growth that never decreases after the action that caused it. Slow growth that plateaus is normal—the heap expands to fit your app's working set. The concern is monotonic increase with no plateau.

items.question: Can React itself leak memory?
items.answer: React itself is careful with memory. Leaks in React apps almost always come from developer-written effects, third-party libraries that hold references, or closures capturing more than needed. React 19's `useEffect` Event pattern reduces listener-leak surface.

items.question: What's a WeakRef and when would you use it?
items.answer: `WeakRef` holds a weak reference to an object—it doesn't prevent garbage collection. You'd use it for a cache where you want entries to expire automatically when memory is tight. It's rarely needed in typical React code; most leaks are better fixed by removing the strong reference entirely.

items.question: How do I find a leak in production without DevTools?
items.answer: Use the Performance API with `memory` (Chrome-only) to get `usedJSHeapSize`. Log it on a schedule and alert when it grows past a threshold. Pair with `performance.now()` timestamps to correlate growth with user actions.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Every `useEffect` that subscribes to something external must return a cleanup function
Use heap snapshots to find what's retained and trace the retainer chain back to your code
Detached DOM nodes point to JS variables that outlived their components
Strict Mode double-invoking effects is your friend—it catches leaks in development
data.takeaway: Memory leaks in React are effect-management bugs. The fix is always the same: clean up.
